summary: Defines a Management Information Base module for managing MPLS traffic engineering fast reroute. It covers the one-to-one backup method and the facility backup method. Network management systems can use it to monitor and configure these backup paths.

plainLanguage.summary: A MIB is a list of dials and meters a manager can check. This one lists the dials for MPLS backup routes, so a manager can see and adjust how traffic reroutes quickly after a break.

subtitle: SNMP management objects for watching and configuring MPLS fast reroute backup paths.

tldr.problem: MPLS traffic engineering fast reroute (RFC 4090) protects tunnels with backup paths, but operators had no standard SNMP objects to see or configure that protection.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three MIB modules: a general one used by any fast reroute node, one for the one-to-one backup method, and one for the facility backup method. They hold tables of constraints, detour LSPs and bypass-protected tunnels.
tldr.outcome: Network management systems can monitor and configure fast reroute through standard SNMP objects, and implementers need only support the module for the method they use. Writable objects need protection, and SNMPv3 is recommended.

today: RFC 6445 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It manages the fast reroute methods of RFC 4090.

sections.title: Purpose and Framework
sections.content:
This memo defines part of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing MPLS-based fast rerouting on Label Switching Routers (LSRs), as defined in RFC 4090. The modules are meant to be used together with RFC 3811, RFC 3812 and RFC 3813.

Like other MIBs, the objects are generally reached through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and written in SMIv2, described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580. Terminology comes from the MPLS architecture and RFC 4090.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers have a control panel that a manager can read over the network. This document adds the part of the panel for backup routes.

sections.title: Three MIB Modules
sections.content:
RFC 4090 describes two approaches to MPLS TE fast reroute: one-to-one backup and facility backup. This RFC defines one module for each, plus a general one.

  • MPLS-FRR-GENERAL-STD-MIB: objects for any LSR implementing fast reroute. It MUST be implemented if either method is.
  • MPLS-FRR-ONE2ONE-STD-MIB: objects for the one-to-one backup method. It MUST be implemented if that method is.
  • MPLS-FRR-FACILITY-STD-MIB: objects for the facility backup method. It MUST be implemented if that method is.

RFC 4090 allows a node to support both methods at once, but the RFC says common practice is that operators configure one or the other at a time. Splitting the MIB lets developers implement only the module for the method their node supports.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to build a backup road. The panel has one page for each way, and a shared page for things both ways need.

sections.title: The General Module
sections.content:
The general module has two scalar objects. mplsFrrGeneralProtectionMethod is read-write and says which method the device uses: unknown(1), oneToOneBackup(2) or facilityBackup(3). Some devices may need a reboot for a change to take effect. mplsFrrGeneralIngressTunnelInstances counts the tunnel instances for detour LSPs or bypass tunnels for which this LSR is the ingress.

The constraints table sets the rules for setting up backup Label Switched Paths (LSPs), such as bandwidth, for a tunnel instance to be protected. It MUST be implemented at the ingress node of the protected tunnel. Its protection type is either linkProtection(1), protecting one link's resources, or nodeProtection(2), protecting a whole node, and its setup priority is in the range 0 to 7.

The hop table extends the mplsTunnelARHopTable of RFC 3812. For each hop of a protected tunnel it records the local protection desired (from the SESSION_ATTRIBUTE flags, such as localProtectionDesired and nodeProtectionDesired) and what is actually available or in use (from the Record Route sub-object flags, such as localProtectionAvailable and localProtectionInUse).
sections.plainLanguage: One dial says which backup style the router uses. Other pages list the rules for each backup road and which roads are already being used.

sections.title: One-to-One Backup Tables
sections.content:
In the one-to-one method each Point of Local Repair (PLR) builds a detour LSP to protect a tunnel instance. The mplsFrrOne2OnePlrTable records the PLRs that started detours. The mplsFrrOne2OneDetourTable shows the detour LSPs in each node (ingress, transit and egress). Both MUST be supported when this method is used.

A detour is identified by the tunnel index (the Tunnel ID of the protected LSP), the tunnel instance, and the ingress and egress LSR IDs. The tunnel instance is split in two: the higher 16 bits are the protected tunnel instance, and the lower 16 bits are the detour instance. A detour LSP is also a tunnel instance, so each one SHOULD have an entry in the mplsTunnelTable of RFC 3812.
sections.plainLanguage: For each stretch of road, a repair spot builds a private detour. The tables list every detour and which main road it protects.

sections.title: Facility Backup and Worked Examples
sections.content:
In facility backup, backup tunnels protect the tunnels that traverse an interface. The mplsFrrFacilityDBTable has one entry for each tunnel protected by a backup tunnel, and the protecting tunnel exists on the PLR as in RFC 4090. Each entry counts the protecting tunnels, protected LSPs and protected tunnels on the interface, and shows the protecting tunnel's reserved bandwidth. Its status is active (label in the LFIB, ready for packets), ready (label entry created but not yet in the LFIB) or partial (label entry not fully created).

The module also has configured and active counts for interfaces and bypass tunnels, plus notifications that are disabled by default (mplsFrrFacilityNotificationsEnabled) and can be throttled with mplsFrrFacilityNotificationsMaxRate.

The RFC walks through small five-router topologies and shows how the tables would be filled in for a link-protecting backup, a one-to-one detour and a facility bypass.
sections.plainLanguage: In this style one big bypass road protects many routes at once. The panel shows if the bypass is ready, almost ready, or already in use.

sections.title: Handling IPv6 Tunnels
sections.content: Following RFC 4990, supporting IPv6 MPLS tunnels in the mplsTunnelTable requires all LSRs in the network to have a 32-bit LSR ID. The ingress and egress LSR ID objects in the one-to-one PLR table, the one-to-one detour table and the facility database table therefore hold a 32-bit LSR ID. They are 32 bits long, like the existing mplsTunnelIngressLSRId and mplsTunnelEgressLSRId.
sections.plainLanguage: Every router gets a short ID number, so the same panel works even when the network uses the newer, longer addresses.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The modules are useful for monitoring, and they can also configure objects, so anything configured can be configured incorrectly, "with potentially disastrous results". Objects with a MAX-ACCESS of read-write or read-create, such as the constraints table and mplsFrrGeneralProtectionMethod, can provision fast reroute, so unauthorized access could disrupt traffic.

Readable objects can also reveal the fast reroute interfaces, tunnels and configuration, so even GET and NOTIFY access should be controlled. SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC RECOMMENDS SNMPv3 with its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says deploying older SNMP versions is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who can turn these dials could break the backup roads, so only trusted people should be allowed to touch or even look at them.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA assigned object identifier values under mib-2 to the three modules: 202 for MPLS-FRR-GENERAL-STD-MIB, 203 for MPLS-FRR-ONE2ONE-STD-MIB and 204 for MPLS-FRR-FACILITY-STD-MIB. These are recorded in the SMI Numbers registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Each page of the panel got its own official number so nobody mixes them up.
